question:
Which of the below has not undergone trisyllabic laxing during its sound development: 

southern, derivative, serenity, pleasant, gratitude, shadow

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is shadow. It derives from Old English sceadu (with an already short /æ/ or similar), and unlike the Latinate forms in the list it shows no evidence of a prior long vowel that would have been subject to trisyllabic laxing in Middle English; the others all display the expected shortening in a _CVCV environment (e.g., serene ~ serenity, derive ~ derivative).

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the classic synchronic/historical sense trisyllabic laxing is the
shortening / laxing of a tense vowel in a stressed syllable when the stressed
syllable is followed by two unstressed syllables, the textbook Latinate
derivation chain

derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvə-]tɪv/
serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnə-]ti/

and the same kind of suffixal shortening is what you get in
gratitude < O.Fr. gratitude, /ˈɡræ.tɪ.tuːd/ with a lax initial /æ/ in a
realis trisyllabic  ˈCV.CV.CV word.

shadow is the Germanic odd man out. It is monomorphemic OE sceadu >
shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/ , a disyllabic native word whose /æ/ is the regular
continuation of OE /æː/ and which never acquires a tense vowel that is
then shortened by the addition of a second unstressed syllable in a
trisyllabic environment. The same purely disyllabic status holds for
southern /ˈsʌ.ðən/ and pleasant /ˈplɛ.zənt/ in modern English, with
pleasant being a Romance borrowing already with an open /ɛ/ in Old French
plaisant.  That is why shadow – and in the strict syllable-count sense
southern / pleasant as well – is normally quoted as not having undergone
the classic Latinate trisyllabic laxing chain that derivative, serenity
and gratitude show.

2.text:
Trisyllabic laxing is the English regular shortening/laxing of a tense
stressed vowel /i:/, /u:/, /eɪ/, /oʊ/ > /ɪ/, /ʊ/, /ɛ/, /ɔ/ when the stressed
syllable is followed by two or more unstressed syllables, and it is
normally illustrated with a disyllabic/tri-syllabic pair.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪv.ə.tɪv/ 
  /aɪ/ > /ɪ/ in the stressed syllable which is now followed by
  -ə.tɪv.
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛ.nə.ti/
  /iː/ > /ɛ/ in the stressed syllable which is now followed by
  -nə.ti.

the same type of vowel shortening is visible in the disyllabic 
please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛ.zənt/  /iː/ > /ɛ/ before a consonant +
schwa, and in the historical shade /ʃeɪd/ > shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/  /eɪ/ > /æ/,
and south /saʊθ/ > southern /ˈsʌ.ðən/  /aʊ/ > /ʌ/.  All of those are
laxings, but only the first two are the canonical trisyllabic
environment.

gratitude /ˈɡræt.ɪ.tuːd/ is a true three-syllable word with stress on
the first syllable followed by two unstressed syllables, but the
stressed vowel is the already lax /æ/.  There is no tense
antecedent /eɪ/, /oʊ/, /iː/, /uː/ to be laxed in the word, so it is the
normal trisyllabic word of the set which simply never shows the
tense → lax alternation.  In the strict syllable-count sense shadow,
pleasant and southern are not trisyllabic at all and therefore cannot
be instances of the trisyllabic rule, the classic non-trisyllabic
example being shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/ < shade /ʃeɪd/.

That is the usual teaching point that gratitude is the genuine
trisyllabic item of the list which has not undergone trisyllabic
laxing.

In English the classic Latinate  trisyllabic laxing is the historically
conditioned laxening of a stressed long vowel /iː uː eɪ oʊ/ > /ɪ ʊ ɛ ɒ/
when the vowel is the stressed vowel of a word of three or more
syllables and the word is most usually a Latinate loan.

That is the

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvə.tɪv/   /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛ.nɪ.ti/   /iː/ > /ɛ/
* grate /greɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡræt.ɪ.tuːd/    /eɪ/ > /æ/

and the same type of laxening that is normally quoted for pleasant
/ˈplɛz.ənt/ < please /pliːz/  etc.

Southern, pleasant and shadow are all disyllabic in Modern English and
are therefore never in the trisyllabic environment which conditions the
classical Latinate laxing.  Of the six items the clear Germanic
disyllable is

* shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/ < OE sceadu

whose first syllable vowel is the regular OE /æː/ > ME /aː/ > ModE /æ/
and which is in no way a Latinate trisyllabic laxing development.
In the same way southern /ˈsʌð.ən/ and pleasant /ˈplɛz.ənt/ are
disyllabic and do not belong to the trisyllabic laxing set, the
unambiguously Latinate trisyllabic laxing examples being derivative,
serenity and gratitude.  This is the sense in which shadow – and in
fact southern and pleasant – is normally quoted as the non-trisyllabic
laxing member of the set.

* grate /ɡreɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪtjuːd/  /eɪ/ > /æ/
* please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/  /iː/ > /ɛ/

in the historical development of the Latinate/French stratum. The vowel is shortened in the polysyllabic derivative/serenity/gratitude/pleasant because the stressed syllable is followed by two unstressed syllables antepenultimate stress.
